_CANON_TXT = "/logs/verifier/reward.txt"

def canon_reward(f2p_passed, f2p_total, p2p_passed, p2p_total, rubric):
    """THE reward policy for the whole corpus. BINARY -- there is no partial credit.

    tests_passed is 1.0 only when every f2p test passes AND every p2p test still passes. A
    strict subset of f2p passing is not partial progress worth scoring: the task is unsolved,
    so it is 0.0.

    reward is the same value, zeroed when the rubric judge failed a criterion. A "pass" or a
    "not graded" verdict never lowers the score -- the judge must never be able to penalise a
    run it could not grade.
    """
    f, t = int(f2p_passed), int(f2p_total)
    p, q = int(p2p_passed), int(p2p_total)
    solved = bool(t) and f == t and p == q
    tests_passed = 1.0 if solved else 0.0
    _canon.clear()

        "reward": 0.0 if rubric == "fail" else tests_passed,
        "tests_passed": tests_passed,
        "f2p_passed": f, "f2p_total": t,
        "p2p_passed": p, "p2p_total": q,
        "rubric_passed": {"pass": 1, "fail": 0}.get(rubric, -1),

## What was wrong

The symptom in the two captures: a screen full of colored cells, and after the window is occluded and brought back to the front (a full repaint), every custom cell color reverts to the default background — **except** the one styled by a CSS *class* (`flagged`, orange), which keeps its color.

The cause is in `Stylesheet.apply()` (`src/textual/css/stylesheet.py`), the **cache key** used to reuse computed CSS rules across similar-looking nodes during a batch stylesheet application (which is what a repaint/refresh triggers, via `update_nodes`):

```python
type(node._parent),                                    # too weak: loses the parent's own id/classes
(None if node._id is None
 else (node._id if f"#{node._id}" not in rules_map else None)),   # drops the id exactly when it matters
```

The `_id` branch is inverted. When an `#id` selector targets a node, its id is precisely what distinguishes it from its siblings — but the code replaced the id with `None` in that case, so two id-styled siblings (e.g. `#four` and `#one`) collapse to the **same** cache entry. The first one computed wins; the rest inherit its rules and lose their own color. Cells styled by a **class** carry a distinct `node.classes` in the key, so they land in their own bucket and survive — which is why only `flagged` kept its look. Keying the parent on `type(...)` instead of the parent object compounds it by merging nodes across different parents.

I verified the collapse directly (`#four` rendered teal instead of red), reproduced the full "lost after repaint" behavior end-to-end with Textual's headless Pilot on the pre-fix code (`off` and `pinned` lost their colors, `flagged` survived), and confirmed the fix keeps all colors stable.

Restore a correct, sufficient cache key — the parent object identity plus the node's own selector-relevant attributes:

```python
cache_key = (
    node._parent,
    node._id,
    node.classes,
    node._pseudo_classes_cache_key,
    node._css_type_name,
)
```

This keeps nodes with different ids in separate cache entries (correctness) while still letting genuinely-identical siblings share (the intended optimization). All 9 runnable stylesheet unit tests pass.
